newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya coffee output seen at four-year low in 96/97.
newsitem.headline: Kenya coffee output seen at four-year low in 96/97.

text.p: Drought sweeping through East Africa will reduce Kenya's coffee production to the lowest levels in four years, senior industry leaders said on Thursday.
A director at the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) told Reuters "The latest estimate by our experts puts the 1996/97 figure at just 78,000 tonnes. Drought is the main culprit for this."

It was the fourth revision of the 1996/97 crop the Coffee Board of Kenya has posted so far. In January, the board forecast production at 85,000 tonnes compared to a final figure of 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95.

"The coffee trees in main growing areas are just drying up. It does not matter even when the fields are irrigated. It's like throwing the crop in the air," a crop pathologist from the Coffee Research Foundation (CRF) told Reuters.
The board director said global prices were good in the past year, fertilisers and insecticides had reached farmers in time and roads to markets had been improved.
"Which means that drought has had a more devastating effect than previously thought," the director added.
Coffee berry disease (CBD) in Kenya'y growing areas in June-July last year also adversely affected production.
Coffee is Kenya's third largest hard currency earner behind tourism and tea and any sharp decline in earnings could undermine its balance of payments position, economists said.
The board director declined to give any export details.
Kenya is Africa's fourth largest coffee producer after Uganda, Ivory Coast and Ethiopia, according to figures from the Abidjan-based Inter-African Coffee Organization (IACO).

Kenya exported 109,372 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 -- including carryover stocks -- earning 16.36 billion shillings ($302.9 million), compared to 79,482 tonnes in 1994/95 worth 14.4 billion shillings.

Prices have risen sharply at Kenya's weekly export auction in recent weeks, due to an anticipated supply shortfalls on the international market, gaining some $20 on strong demand for good quality arabica coffees. Premium grade ABs averaged $291 per 50-kg (110 lb) from $268 while grade AAs averaged $296 from $274. Grade Cs averaged $279 from $261.
"A general shortage of coffee in the overseas market has been pushing prices up this year," said a trader, adding that the current crop on offer was very high quality.
Traders added that since there was no real substitute for Kenyan coffee, prices would continue to climb and any shortfall in domestic output would only raise levels further.
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi has declared the drought a national disaster and appealed for international food aid. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
